title: Per-session role cache, sized for short web sessions, reused for 8-hour impersonation
diff: -        # Always reflects the current DB state -- a role revocation
-        # takes effect on the very next request.
+        # Hot endpoints call this on every request; a DB round-trip per
+        # request was measurably expensive. Cache once per session and
+        # let callers that need a live check bypass the cache
+    """Support agents can act as a customer to reproduce a reported
+    bug. The impersonation session is scoped to the target user's own
+    permissions, exactly as if the target user had logged in
+- New support-only "impersonate user" tool, letting a support agent
+  reproduce a customer-reported bug from inside the customer's own
+  account. Sessions expire automatically after 8 hours and every
+  impersonation start is written to the audit log.
+- Role lookups on the request-scoped session are now cached per
+  session instead of hitting the DB on every request.

ground_truth.explanation: permissions.py's checks are correct both before and after. session.py's role caching is a reasonable trade for its original use case: a normal web session where a DB round trip per request was the actual cost problem, and refresh_roles() exists as an explicit escape hatch. impersonation.py is new and, on its own, correctly scopes a support session to the target user's permissions at the moment impersonation starts. Nothing in this diff calls refresh_roles() for impersonation sessions, and those sessions can live up to MAX_IMPERSONATION_HOURS (8). If the target user's roles are revoked mid-impersonation -- exactly the scenario a security incident would trigger -- the support agent keeps operating with the pre-revocation cached roles for up to 8 more hours.
